make for.verb type: **both** — action in sense 1, dynamic physical movement toward a goal (*she made for the exit*). Sense 2 is **stative**, a situation standing in a relation to its result, and it resists the progressive: ✗ *rain is making for a sloppy game*.
make for.passive: **no** — the prepositional passive fails in both senses: ✗ *the exit was made for*, ✗ *a long day is made for by two connecting flights*.

make of.verb type: action — dynamic but mental, the act of forming or voicing an opinion. No stative or linking use; the frame needs both a *what / much / nothing* object and an *of* phrase.
make of.passive: **restricted** — natural only in sense 2, where the quantity is promoted: *a great deal was made of one careless sentence*. Sense 1 has no passive at all: ✗ *what is made of the new manager?*

make off.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of hurried escape, always with a human or animal subject. No stative or linking use.
make off.passive: **no** — intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *was made off*, ✗ *the alley was made off down*.

make off with.verb type: action — dynamic and agentive: taking something and fleeing with it. No stative or linking use.
make off with.passive: **restricted** — the three-part passive is marginal in American English: ?*my bike was made off with*, ✗ *it was made off with by a kid*. Say *was stolen* instead.

make out.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 2–5 (faring, writing out a check, claiming, kissing). Sense 1 is a **perception** verb close to stative: it lives with *can / could* and avoids the progressive, ✗ *I am making out a figure*.
make out.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the signature could barely be made out*, *the check was made out to the county clerk*, *he was made out to be some kind of expert*. Intransitive senses 2 and 5 have none: ✗ *was made out at the DMV*.

make over.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, the physical transformation and the legal transfer of property. No stative or linking use.
make over.passive: **yes**, and common in both — *the basement was made over into a rec room*; *the farm had been made over to a trust years before he died*.

make up.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 1 and 3–6 (inventing, reconciling, catching up, applying cosmetics, preparing). Sense 2, 'constitute', is **stative** and refuses the progressive: ✗ *volunteers are making up half the staff*.
make up.passive: **restricted** — fine in the dynamic senses: *the story was made up on the drive over*, *the prescription was made up in ten minutes*, *she was made up for the stage lights*. Sense 2 passivizes only in the fixed *be made up of* — *the district is made up of six counties*, never ✗ *made up by six counties* — and sense 3 is intransitive: ✗ *she was made up with*.

make up for.verb type: **both** — action when a person compensates (*she worked doubles to make up for the time off*), **stative** when a thing simply offsets another, where the progressive is odd: *the view makes up for the stairs*, ✗ *the view is making up for the stairs*.
make up for.passive: **restricted** — stiff at best, and only with the loss as subject: ?*the lost time will be made up for*. ✗ *the stairs are made up for by the view*.

make up to.verb type: action — dynamic and agentive, flattering somebody for gain; the object is always a person. British, where American English says *suck up to* or *butter up*.
make up to.passive: **no** — ✗ *the department head was made up to*, ✗ *she was made up to by the neighbors*. The prepositional passive is simply unavailable here.

meet up.verb type: action — dynamic, an arranged social get-together. No stative or linking use.
meet up.passive: **no** — intransitive, so no passive exists: ✗ *was met up at the taco place*. Use plain *meet* if you need one: *we were met at the gate*.

meet up with.verb type: action — dynamic, a planned joining-up with somebody; never a chance encounter, which is *run into*.
meet up with.passive: **no** — ✗ *my cousin was met up with in Chicago*, ✗ *they had been met up with twice*. Recast with plain *meet*: *she was met at baggage claim*.

meet with.verb type: **both** — action in sense 1, an agentive scheduled meeting (*the governor met with tribal leaders*). Sense 2 is non-agentive and near-stative: the subject undergoes a reception rather than doing anything.
meet with.passive: **no** in either sense — ✗ *tribal leaders were met with on Monday*, ✗ *stiff resistance was met with by the proposal*. Do not be fooled by *the proposal was met with resistance*: that is the passive of plain transitive *meet* plus a *with* phrase, not of this verb.

pay back.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, repaying money and getting even. No stative or linking use.
pay back.passive: **yes**, with either object promoted — *the loan was paid back two years early*; *she was paid back for every remark she ever made*.

pay down.verb type: action — dynamic, and gradual by definition, so the progressive is natural: *we're paying the card down before the rate resets*.
pay down.passive: **yes** — *the balance was paid down to under a thousand*, *half of the pension shortfall has been paid down*.

pay for.verb type: **both** — action in sense 1, an agentive handing over of money. Sense 2 is non-agentive, the subject suffering a consequence, and sense 3 (*pay for itself*) is a fixed reflexive idiom with an inanimate subject.
pay for.passive: **restricted** — excellent in sense 1: *the whole wedding was paid for by her parents*, *two more technicians are paid for by the grant*. Sense 2 is marginal (?*that remark will be paid for*) and sense 3 has none, being reflexive: ✗ *itself was paid for by the furnace*.

pay off.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: clearing a debt, bribing, dismissing with severance, and, in intransitive sense 3, an effort finally yielding a result.
pay off.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the house was paid off in eleven years*, *the inspector had been paid off*, *half the yard staff were paid off when the contract ended*. Sense 3 is intransitive: ✗ *the gamble was paid off*.

pay out.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, disbursing a sum and feeding out rope; the money sense often leaves the object unstated (*a machine that never pays out*).
pay out.passive: **yes** — *about ninety thousand dollars was paid out on the policy*; *the cable was paid out slowly so it would not kink*.

pay up.verb type: action — dynamic, and usually a demand; the bare imperative *pay up* is its commonest form.
pay up.passive: **no** — intransitive, so nothing can be promoted: ✗ *the money was paid up*, ✗ *the tenants were paid up*. Use *pay off* or *pay back* when a passive is needed.

put across.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of getting an idea to land. Often with *can / could*, but freely progressive: *she's putting it across well*.
put across.passive: **yes** — *a difficult argument was put across in ten minutes*, *his point was never quite put across to the committee*.

put aside.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, setting money by and shelving a feeling or a dispute. No stative or linking use.
put aside.passive: **yes** — *two hundred dollars was put aside every month*; *a thirty-year quarrel was put aside for the funeral*.

put away.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: tidying, imprisoning or committing, and eating a great deal.
put away.passive: **yes** — *the winter coats were put away in April*; *he was put away for nine years*; and informally *a whole pie was put away in one sitting*.

put back.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: returning a thing, pushing a date later, resetting a clock, and drinking fast.
put back.passive: **yes** — *the hearing was put back to October*, *the clocks are put back on Sunday*, *an empty carton had been put back on the shelf*.

put by.verb type: action — dynamic, a repeated act of saving against a future need. Old-fashioned and mostly British; no stative or linking use.
put by.passive: **yes**, though most often as a bare participle — *there was nothing put by when the mill closed*, *enough had been put by to cover a bad winter*.

put down.verb type: action — dynamic in all six senses: setting down, belittling, euthanizing, suppressing, recording, and paying a deposit. The noun *a putdown* comes from sense 2.
put down.passive: **yes**, and very common — *the rebellion was put down in a week*, *the old horse was put down in the spring*, *her maiden name was put down by mistake*, *ten percent was put down on the house*.

put down to.verb type: action — dynamic but mental, the act of assigning a cause. The progressive is fine: *I'm putting it down to nerves*.
put down to.passive: **yes** — the entry's own example shows it: *most of the drop can be put down to the weather*; likewise *his rudeness was put down to nerves*.

put forward.verb type: action — dynamic and agentive in both senses, proposing something for judgment and moving a clock or a date earlier. Formal register.
put forward.passive: **yes**, and in writing the passive is the usual shape — *the theory was first put forward in 1911*, *clocks are put forward an hour in March*.

put in.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: installing, submitting, contributing hours, interjecting a remark, and (intransitively, of a boat) stopping at a port.
put in.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *a new water heater was put in last fall*, *a claim was put in the day after the storm*, *twelve years were put in at the plant*. Sense 5 is intransitive: ✗ *Norfolk was put in at*.

put in for.verb type: action — dynamic and agentive, applying formally at work; the subject is always a person.
put in for.passive: **no** — the three-part prepositional passive fails: ✗ *the transfer was put in for*, ✗ *overtime had been put in for by three people*. Recast with *apply for*: *the same shift was applied for by three people*.

put off.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 1 and 3, postponing and stalling. Sense 2 is causative and non-agentive — the subject is whatever repels, not an actor — and gives the adjective *off-putting*.
put off.passive: **yes** — *the wedding was put off until spring*, *going to the dentist has been put off since March*; and sense 2 lives mainly in the passive: *she was put off by how quickly they wanted an answer*.

put on.verb type: action — dynamic in all six senses: dressing, switching on, gaining weight, staging a show, teasing, and feigning a manner.
put on.passive: **yes** in most senses — *a musical is put on every March*, *the porch light was put on*, *you're being put on*. The clothing sense passivizes only when somebody else does the dressing (*the child's boots were put on for her*); ?*her boots were put on at the door* is odd of a self-dresser.

put out.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 1–3 and 5. Sense 4 is not a working verb but a **participial adjective** after a copula: *she seemed put out*, *he looked put out*.
put out.passive: **yes** — *the fire was put out with a dish towel*, *a statement was put out that afternoon*, *the trash gets put out Sunday night*. Sense 4 exists only in that passive shape: *she was clearly put out that nobody had asked her*.

put through.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: connecting a call, making somebody endure an ordeal, funding an education, and getting a deal completed.
put through.passive: **yes**, and it is the normal form with a person as subject — *I was put through to billing*, *every recruit is put through the same week of tests*, *the loan was put through in three days*.

put together.verb type: action — dynamic, assembling from parts or compiling from scratch. Sense 3, *the other three put together*, is a frozen participial tag rather than a live verb.
put together.passive: **yes** — *the crib was put together in four hours*, *the proposal was put together over the weekend*, *the whole shed was put together from a kit*.

put up.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: erecting, posting a notice, housing a guest, supplying money, offering resistance, and putting something up for sale.
put up.passive: **yes** — *a fence was put up along the property line*, *a notice was put up about the water shutoff*, *we were put up for three nights*, *most of the money was put up by two investors*, *the house was put up for sale in July*.

put up with.verb type: action in form — the progressive is fine, *I'm putting up with it for now* — though what it reports is closer to a state of tolerating than to anything done.
put up with.passive: **restricted** — possible but stiff, and best with an inanimate subject: *that kind of noise should not have to be put up with*. ?*He was put up with for a decade* is grammatical but unidiomatic; Americans recast with *tolerate*.

put upon.verb type: action in form, but it survives almost only as a **participial adjective** after a copula — *feel put upon*, *seem put upon*. The active *put upon her* is formal and rare.
put upon.passive: **yes**, and the passive is effectively the only living form — *he was put upon for years and never said a word*, *nobody likes being put upon by a stranger*, *she is easily put upon*.

quit on.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, a person walking out on somebody and a machine failing at the worst moment. Informal spoken American.
quit on.passive: **no** — ✗ *the coach was quit on by half the roster*, ✗ *I was quit on by the truck*. The verb is fixed in the active, with the person let down after *on*.

read back.verb type: action — dynamic, reading something aloud so it can be checked; standard on the phone, in cockpits, and in courtrooms.
read back.passive: **yes** — *the witness's last answer was read back*, *the clearance has to be read back to the tower*.

read into.verb type: action — dynamic but mental, finding a meaning that was probably never there. Usually negative or with *too much*.
read into.passive: **restricted** — only the quantity phrase can be promoted: *too much has been read into one bad review*, *far more was read into the phrasing than the author intended*. ✗ *her silence was read into*, because *into* keeps its own object.

read off.verb type: **action — dynamic**. A physical act of reading aloud off a display or a label, so the progressive is natural: *she was reading off the serial numbers as he typed*.
read off.passive: **yes**, and it is common in reports of procedure: *the numbers were read off one at a time*, *his blood pressure was read off without comment*.

read out.verb type: **action — dynamic**. Reading aloud to a group, an event with a beginning and an end: *the clerk was reading out the names when we came in*.
read out.passive: **yes**, and very natural — this is the standard way to report it: *the verdict was read out at four*, *the terms were read out before anyone signed*.

read over.verb type: **action — dynamic**. Checking something by reading it once through, a deliberate act: *she was reading over the contract when he called*.
read over.passive: **yes** — *the contract was read over twice before anyone signed*, *my cover letter was read over and cut by two paragraphs*.

read through.verb type: **action — dynamic**. A single complete pass from beginning to end, so it is often perfective: *I had read through the whole manual by midnight*.
read through.passive: **yes** — *the script was read through on the first morning*, *every file had been read through by midnight*.

read up on.verb type: **action — dynamic**. Deliberate private study over a stretch of time: *she was reading up on the procedure all week*.
read up on.passive: **restricted** — the three-part frame passivizes stiffly. ?*the tax rules were read up on before he filed* is grammatical but nobody says it; ✗ *it was read up on by her* is worse. Keep it active.

ride on.verb type: **stative** in meaning — it names a relation of dependency, not an act: *a lot rides on Thursday's vote*. Unusually for a stative it prefers the progressive, which here marks the state, not an activity: *three hundred jobs are riding on the contract*.
ride on.passive: **no** — the subject is the stake and *on* will not release its object: ✗ *Thursday's vote is being ridden on by a lot*, ✗ *the contract is ridden on by three hundred jobs*.

ride out.verb type: **action — dynamic**, though what it describes is endurance rather than activity: you *ride out* a storm by waiting: *they were riding out the hurricane in the basement*.
ride out.passive: **restricted** — grammatical but stiff, and the active is overwhelmingly preferred: ?*the recession was ridden out on two contracts*, ?*the scandal was ridden out*. Say *they rode it out*.

ride up.verb type: **action — dynamic**, with an inanimate subject that does the moving: the garment works its way upward on its own. Habitual present is the usual tense: *this skirt rides up every time I sit down*.
ride up.passive: **no** — intransitive, with no object anywhere to promote: ✗ *the knee is ridden up at by cheap leggings*.

ring back.verb type: **action — dynamic**; the act of returning a call. Transitive or intransitive with no change of meaning: *he'll ring back*, *he'll ring you back*.
ring back.passive: **restricted** — the transitive use will passivize in British English (*she was rung back within the hour*) but it is rare and the active is standard. No passive at all of the intransitive *he rang back twice*.

ring in.verb type: **action — dynamic** in both senses — the celebratory *ring in the new year* and the British *ring in sick* are each things people do at a moment: *they were ringing in the new year on the roof*.
ring in.passive: **yes** in sense 1, where there is an object: *the new year was rung in with a fish fry*. **No** in sense 2, which takes no object: ✗ *sick was rung in by two of the drivers*.

ring off.verb type: **action — dynamic** — a single punctual act, the end of a call: *she rang off before I could ask*. It takes the progressive only in the sense of being about to: *I'm ringing off now*.
ring off.passive: **no** — objectless, so nothing can be promoted to subject: ✗ *the call was rung off*, ✗ *I was rung off on*.

ring out.verb type: **action — dynamic** in sense 1, with the sound itself as subject: *a single shot rang out*. Sense 2 (*ring out the old year*) is dynamic and transitive but frozen into that one phrase.
ring out.passive: **no** in sense 1 — it has no object: ✗ *the field was rung out across by a shot*. **Restricted** in sense 2: *the old year is rung out on the same bell* is possible but ceremonial, and outside that phrase it does not occur.

ring up.verb type: **action — dynamic** in all three senses — entering a sale, racking up a total, or (British) telephoning. All take the progressive: *she was ringing up two coffees*.
ring up.passive: **yes**, and it is idiomatic in senses 1 and 2: *the whole order was rung up wrong*, *thirty-one points were rung up in the first half*. The British telephone sense passivizes only awkwardly: ?*I was rung up by his office*.

rise above.verb type: **action — dynamic** in both senses, though nothing physical moves — refusing to stoop (*rise above it*) and overcoming a disadvantage (*the film rises above a thin script*) are both achievements rather than states.
rise above.passive: **no** — *rise* is intransitive and *above* keeps its object: ✗ *the sniping was risen above by her*, ✗ *a thin script is risen above by the film*.

rise to.verb type: **action — dynamic** — an achievement at a particular moment, whether creditable (*rose to the occasion when the power failed*) or not (*half the room rose to it*).
rise to.passive: **no** — the verb is intransitive, so the object of *to* cannot move: ✗ *the occasion was risen to by the whole crew*, ✗ *the bait was risen to*.

rise up.verb type: **action — dynamic** in the rebellion sense (*the provinces rose up against the new tax*). The literary sense 2 is closer to a **stative** description of landscape, in the habitual present: *the ridge rises up out of flat country*.
rise up.passive: **no** — intransitive in both senses, with the rebels or the cliff as subject: ✗ *the new tax was risen up against*, ✗ *flat country is risen up out of*.

run across.verb type: **action — dynamic**, but purely accidental and momentary, so the progressive is odd: ✗ *I am running across an old photo*. Use it in the simple past: *I ran across it in a library book*.
run across.passive: **no** — this is the textbook prepositional verb that will not passivize: ✗ *an old photo was run across in a library book*, ✗ *he was run across at a gas station*.

run after.verb type: **action — dynamic** in all three senses — chasing on foot, pursuing romantically, and waiting on somebody — and all three take the progressive: *he spent two years running after her*.
run after.passive: **restricted** — the literal chase resists it (✗ *the bus was run after for half a block*), but the romantic sense passivizes in the abstract: *she has no interest in being run after*.

run along.verb type: **action — dynamic**, and almost frozen in the imperative: *run along now*. Outside commands and reported commands it barely appears.
run along.passive: **no** — no object at all: ✗ *the kids were run along*, ✗ *it was run along by the children*.

run around.verb type: **action — dynamic**, and characteristically progressive because it describes ongoing scattered activity: *she has been running around since six*.
run around.passive: **no** — the verb takes no object of its own: ✗ *all morning was run around*. Even the prepositional *run around on somebody* stays active: ✗ *she was being run around on* — say *he was cheating on her*.

run away.verb type: **action — dynamic** in both senses — fleeing a place (*he ran away twice before fifteen*) and avoiding a problem (*he runs away from every conversation that matters*).
run away.passive: **no** — intransitive throughout: ✗ *home was run away from by him*, ✗ *a bill like that can't be run away from*.

run away with.verb type: **action — dynamic** in all four senses. Sense 4 is the odd one: the feeling is the subject and the person the object — *don't let your imagination run away with you*.
run away with.passive: **restricted**, and marginal in practice: ✗ *the whole tip jar was run away with*, ✗ *he was run away with by a bass player*. Sports writing will occasionally allow *the game was run away with in the third quarter*, but the active is the safe choice.

run by.verb type: **action — dynamic** — a deliberate act of consultation: *I was running it by legal all last week*. The frame needs both an object and a *by* phrase.
run by.passive: **yes**, and it is genuinely idiomatic in American workplace English: *the plan was run by legal before anyone signed*, *has this been run by the client yet?* The agent, when named, needs a second *by*: *it was run by legal by his assistant* — clumsy, so leave the agent out.

run down.verb type: **action — dynamic** throughout: hitting somebody with a vehicle, belittling them, tracking a thing down, or going through a list. Sense 3 (*the battery had run down*) is a dynamic change of state with the battery as subject.
run down.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses, and common in senses 1 and 4: *two cyclists were run down on the shoulder*, *the original invoice was finally run down*, *she was run down by her own department*. **No** passive of sense 3: ✗ *the battery was run down overnight* can only mean somebody drained it.

run for.verb type: **action — dynamic**, and often durative — a whole campaign, not a moment: *she is running for city council this spring*. The fixed *run for it* (sense 2) is punctual instead.
run for.passive: **no** — the office cannot become the subject: ✗ *mayor is being run for by him*, ✗ *reelection has not been run for since 2016*.

run in.verb type: **action — dynamic** in both senses — hauling somebody to the station, and the British *run the engine in* gently over the first thousand miles.
run in.passive: **yes**, and the entry's own example is a passive: *he got run in for something that would not even be a ticket now*, *the engine should be run in gently before you tow anything*.

run into.verb type: **action — dynamic** in senses 1 to 3, but accidental, so the progressive marks habit rather than an event in progress: *she runs into him at the same coffee shop twice a week*. Sense 4 (*repairs could run into six figures*) is **stative** — a measurement, not an act: ✗ *repairs are running into six figures*.
run into.passive: **no** in the chance-meeting and problem senses — ✗ *my old roommate was run into at the airport*, ✗ *the same problem has been run into every quarter*. The collision sense is marginal at best: ?*the guardrail was run into by a truck in the fog*.

run off.verb type: **action — dynamic** in every sense — fleeing (1), copying (2), driving somebody away (3), and water draining (4). Sense 4 takes an inanimate subject: *the rain runs off the clay*.
run off.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses 2 and 3: *thirty copies were run off before the meeting*, *they were run off his land twice*. **No** in senses 1 and 4, which have no object: ✗ *Reno was run off to*, ✗ *the clay is run off by the rain*.

run off with.verb type: **action — dynamic** in both senses — eloping with a person and making off with a thing. Punctual, so the past is its home tense: *the treasurer ran off with eleven thousand dollars*.
run off with.passive: **no** — like the other three-part verbs of taking, it will not promote its object: ✗ *eleven thousand dollars was run off with by the treasurer*, ✗ *the good scissors were run off with again*.

run on.verb type: **action — dynamic** in senses 1 and 2 (a meeting running long, a person talking on), both naturally progressive: *the trial had been running on for eleven weeks*. Sense 3, *run on propane*, is **stative** — a permanent property of the machine: ✗ *the generator is running on propane* means it is doing so right now, not what it is built for.
run on.passive: **no** — objectless in senses 1 and 2, and the fuel will not move to subject in sense 3: ✗ *propane is run on by the generator*, ✗ *diesel is still run on by half the fleet*.

run out.verb type: **action — dynamic** — a change of state, with the supply or the period as subject: *the milk ran out before breakfast*, *her lease runs out in June*. The progressive means approaching the end: *we're running out*.
run out.passive: **no** — intransitive, and the supply is already the subject: ✗ *the milk was run out*, ✗ *her lease was run out in June*. For a personal subject the verb has to add a preposition: *we ran out of milk*.

run out of.verb type: **action — dynamic** — a change of state reached at a point in time: *I ran out of gas two exits from home*. The progressive means nearly: *we're running out of chairs*.
run out of.passive: **no** — the exhausted supply cannot become the subject: ✗ *gas was run out of two exits from home*, ✗ *excuses had been run out of by the third week*.

run out on.verb type: **action — dynamic** — abandoning somebody at a moment: *he ran out on his family in 1989*. Reproachful, so it is nearly always a past-tense accusation.
run out on.passive: **restricted** — it occurs but reads stiffly: ?*she was run out on by the only investor she trusted*. Americans say *she was walked out on* or, better, keep it active: *he ran out on her*.

run over.verb type: **action — dynamic** in all four senses: hitting something with a car (1), going past a time limit (2), reviewing quickly (3), and overflowing (4). Senses 2 and 4 take the situation or the container as subject: *the meeting ran over*, *the sink ran over*.
run over.passive: **yes** in sense 1, where it is the ordinary way to say it: *the mailbox was run over during the storm*, *the dog got run over on Route 9*. **No** in senses 2 and 4, which have no object: ✗ *twenty minutes were run over*. Sense 3 passivizes only awkwardly: ?*the agenda was run over one more time*.

run through.verb type: **action — dynamic** in senses 1, 2, and 4 — rehearsing, spending fast, and the archaic piercing with a blade. Sense 3, *a streak of stubbornness runs through that family*, is **stative**: it describes a standing property, not an event, and rejects the progressive (✗ *is running through that family*).
run through.passive: **yes** in senses 1 and 4, and the entry's own example is one: *he was run through in the second act*, *the safety checks were run through twice*. Sense 2 is acceptable but stiff (?*the whole advance was run through in four months*), and sense 3 has no passive: ✗ *that family is run through by a streak of stubbornness*.

run up.verb type: **action — dynamic** in all three senses — piling up charges, hoisting a flag, and sewing something quickly. Sense 1 is gradual and takes the progressive well: *he was running up a tab all night*.
run up.passive: **yes**, and idiomatic in every transitive sense: *a four-hundred-dollar tab was run up in one evening*, *the flag is run up at seven every morning*, *the whole dress was run up in an afternoon*.

run up against.verb type: **action — dynamic** — meeting an obstacle at a point in time, with the project or the person as subject: *the project ran up against the zoning board in its first month*.
run up against.passive: **no** — the obstacle stays where it is: ✗ *the zoning board was run up against by the project*, ✗ *the same objection was run up against at every meeting*.

run with.verb type: **action — dynamic** — taking an idea and developing it, usually over a stretch of time: *she was running with the suggestion before anyone approved it*.
run with.passive: **no** — the idea cannot be promoted: ✗ *the suggestion was run with by her*, ✗ *the joke was run with by somebody in marketing*. Keep it active, or say *the suggestion was taken up*.
